Lab 1 code¶

This notebook contains the code, the figures and the answers to the questions of the lab. The run-by-run record (hypothesis, change, validation result, conclusion) is in logbook.md.

1. Initialization¶

In this section we import the proper libraries and define a seed

In [1]:
import copy, time, random
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.optim as optim
from IPython.display import display
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder, StandardScaler, RobustScaler, FunctionTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, confusion_matrix, f1_score, recall_score, ConfusionMatrixDisplay

SEED = 42
DATA_PATH = "dataset_lab_1.csv"
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
print(device)

def set_seed(seed):
    # The same seed must always produce the same run.
    random.seed(seed); np.random.seed(seed); torch.manual_seed(seed)
    torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)
    torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True
    torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False

def load_raw(csv_path):
    # Read the csv once. Some column names start with a space.
    df = pd.read_csv(csv_path)
    df.columns = df.columns.str.strip()
    return df

def issue_masks(df):
    # One mask per kind of bad row, so that the analysis and prepare_data
    # never disagree on what has to be removed.
    num = df.drop(columns=["Label"])
    num_box = num.replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan)
    return dict(nan=df.isna().any(axis=1),
                inf=np.isinf(num).any(axis=1),
                negative=(num_box < 0).any(axis=1))

cpu

2. Task 1: Preprocessing¶

Before training anything we look at the raw data, clean it, split it and decide how to scale the features. All these steps are implemented in prepare_data, so that every experiment of the lab starts from exactly the same data and the only thing that changes between experiments is the model. The drop_port and drop_duplicates flags allow the following tasks to obtain the dataset without the destination port and/or without deduplication.

2.1. Cleaning¶

Q: How many samples do you have before and after your cleaning?

31507 rows before cleaning and 29384 after: 2123 rows (6.7%) are removed and 93.3% of the data is kept. The steps remove very different amounts, which is why prepare_data reports them one by one:

Step Rows removed
inf -> NaN, then rows with NaN 27
negative values 2
duplicate rows 2094

The order matters. Infinite values are turned into NaN and dropped together with the other missing values, then the rows with negative values go, then the destination port is dropped (optional) and only at the end the duplicate rows are removed, because removing the port creates new duplicates. The duplicate removal alone accounts for 2094 of the 2123 rows, and it does not hit all classes equally: DoS Hulk loses 1132 of its 5000 rows, Benign 760 of 20000, PortScan 151 and Brute Force 80.

The inspection also shows that there is no constant column, but two pairs of features are identical (Fwd PSH Flags = SYN Flag Count and Subflow Fwd Packets = Total Fwd Packets): one column of each pair carries no additional information. We keep them, because duplicated inputs do not harm a feed-forward network and the column layout stays identical to the data used in Task 3.

The labels are then encoded as integers, the data is split 70/15/15 with stratification, and the features are transformed with log1p + StandardScaler fitted on the training set only (the choice is justified in 2.5). prepare_data returns both the transformed arrays (X) and the untouched ones (Xraw), which are needed for the "no scaling" experiment of Task 2B and for the counterfactual test of Task 3.

In [4]:
def prepare_data(csv_path, drop_port=False, drop_duplicates=True, seed=SEED):
    # Read the csv and keep the class counts after every step, to report how many rows are removed.
    df = load_raw(csv_path)
    counts = {"raw": df["Label"].value_counts()}

    # 1) Drop the rows with an infinite or a missing value.
    masks = issue_masks(df)
    df = df[~(masks["inf"] | masks["nan"])]
    counts["after_nan"] = df["Label"].value_counts()

    # 2) Drop the rows with negative values.
    df = df[~issue_masks(df)["negative"]]
    counts["after_negatives"] = df["Label"].value_counts()

    # 3) Optional: drop the destination port.
    if drop_port:
        df = df.drop(columns=["Destination Port"])
    # 4) Optional: drop duplicate rows. Done last, because dropping the port creates new duplicates.
    if drop_duplicates:
        df = df.drop_duplicates()

    counts["after_clean"] = df["Label"].value_counts()

    # Encode the labels as integers.
    le = LabelEncoder()
    y = le.fit_transform(df["Label"].values)
    feature_names = [c for c in df.columns if c != "Label"]
    X = df[feature_names].values

    # Split 70% train, 15% validation, 15% test. Stratify keeps the class proportions.
    Xtr, Xtmp, ytr, ytmp = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=seed, stratify=y)
    Xva, Xte, yva, yte = train_test_split(Xtmp, ytmp, test_size=0.5, random_state=seed, stratify=ytmp)

    # log1p has no parameters, so it is safe on every split.
    # The StandardScaler is fitted on the training data only, to avoid leakage.
    scaler = Pipeline([
        ("log1p", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p)),
        ("standardize", StandardScaler()),
    ]).fit(Xtr)

    # Return the raw arrays (used by the no-scaling test) and the scaled ones.
    raw = dict(train=Xtr, val=Xva, test=Xte)
    return dict(
        Xraw=raw,
        X={k: scaler.transform(v) for k, v in raw.items()},
        y=dict(train=ytr, val=yva, test=yte),
        class_names=list(le.classes_), feature_names=feature_names,
        scaler=scaler, counts=pd.DataFrame(counts))

2.2. Class balance and feature distributions after cleaning¶

29384 flows are left (from 31507): Brute Force stays the smallest class with 1427 flows (4.9%), so the imbalance is unchanged and the stratified split is still needed. The histograms plot every feature of the cleaned training set with a logarithmic y-axis, otherwise the few values in the tails would not be visible. The long right tails visible in the raw boxplots are still there: this is exactly what log1p has to compress.

2.3. Stratified vs random split¶

Since Brute Force is less than 5% of the data, a random split could concentrate a sizeable share of it in a single partition. Both calls to train_test_split are therefore stratified, so every partition keeps the class proportions of the whole dataset. To show that it makes a difference, the same split (same seed) is repeated without stratify and the class shares are compared. Both panels use the same seed and the same proportions as the split used in the rest of the lab; split_proportions re-draws the split from the labels, so the left panel shows the same proportions, not literally the same rows.

In [7]:
# Compare the same split with and without stratification.
class_names_arr = np.array(D["class_names"])
# The three splits together rebuild the labels of the cleaned dataset.
y_all = np.concatenate([D["y"]["train"], D["y"]["val"], D["y"]["test"]])


# Same split, same seed. stratify is None when stratified is False.
def split_proportions(stratified):
    y_tr, y_tmp = train_test_split(y_all, test_size=0.3, random_state=SEED,
                                   stratify=y_all if stratified else None)
    y_va, y_te = train_test_split(y_tmp, test_size=0.5, random_state=SEED,
                                  stratify=y_tmp if stratified else None)
    return pd.DataFrame({
        name: pd.Series(class_names_arr[yy]).value_counts(normalize=True) * 100
        for name, yy in [("train", y_tr), ("val", y_va), ("test", y_te)]
    })


# Left: the stratified split used in the lab. Right: a random split, for comparison.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4), sharex=True)
for ax, stratified, title in [(axes[0], True, "Stratified split"), (axes[1], False, "Random split")]:
    shares = split_proportions(stratified)
    # Percentage of each class in train, validation and test.
    shares.plot.barh(ax=ax, legend=(ax is axes[0]), width=0.8)
    for cont in ax.containers:
        ax.bar_label(cont, fmt=" %.2f%%", fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlabel("% of the partition", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_ylabel("")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=12)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=10)
axes[0].set_xlim(0, shares.values.max() * 1.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
plt.close()

Q: Given the class balance, should the split be stratified? Why? Where did you fit the scaler, and what goes wrong if you fit it on all the data?

Yes: Brute Force is 4.8% of the flows, so a random split can put too many or too few of them in one partition; stratifying keeps the class shares in train (20568), validation (4408) and test (4408). The scaler is fitted on the training partition only. log1p has no parameters, while StandardScaler learns mean and standard deviation there; fitted on all the data, those statistics would also depend on the test set and the test score would stop being an honest estimate on unseen traffic.

2.4. Scaling: comparison of three candidates¶

The boxplots of the raw data show the problem: the features have very different ranges and long right tails (ports, byte counts and durations reach $10^4$-$10^8$ while the bulk of the values stays near zero). We compare three options, all fitted on the training set only: StandardScaler (the one used in the class example), RobustScaler (subtracts the median and divides by the interquartile range) and log1p followed by StandardScaler. In the title of each panel we report the median interquartile range over the features and the largest absolute value after scaling.

In [8]:

2.5. Chosen scaling: log1p + StandardScaler¶

Q: Which scaling did you pick and why? How did the outliers inform the choice?

log1p followed by StandardScaler. StandardScaler alone divides by the standard deviation, which is inflated by the extreme tails: the central 50% of the features ends up squeezed into a median IQR of 0.16 and the largest scaled value is 138, so the bulk of the samples collapses around zero and the network sees almost no variation in the range where 99% of the data lives. RobustScaler keeps the bulk at IQR = 1.00 and is therefore better, but it only rescales: the shape of the distribution does not change, so the tails still reach $1.4 \cdot 10^4$ in scaled units and a few extreme flows keep dominating the gradient. log1p attacks the cause: the features are counts, durations and rates with long right tails, and the logarithm makes them roughly symmetric, after which standardization leaves a usable dynamic range (median IQR 1.53, largest value 11 instead of $1.4 \cdot 10^4$).

The whole transform is fitted on the training set only and then applied to validation and test. log1p has no parameters to learn, so applying it to every partition causes no leakage; if the StandardScaler were fitted on the whole dataset, its mean and standard deviation would also depend on the test set and the test results would no longer be a fair estimate on unseen traffic. In prepare_data the two steps are wrapped in a single Pipeline, so the exact same transform is applied to any new array, e.g. the counterfactual test set of Task 3.

3. Helper functions¶

To help us with the following experiments, we define a set of auxiliary utility functions: The model architecture and optimization setup are managed by build_model and build_optimizer, which dynamically construct multi-layer perceptrons with configurable hidden dimensions, activation functions, dropout rates, and batch normalization alongside AdamW or SGD optimizers. Data ingestion is handled by make_loaders, converting data splits into PyTorch DataLoader instances with deterministic seed generators. Model training is executed through fit, which manages the training loop, tracks training and validation loss and macro-F1 scores, applies early stopping, and restores the best model checkpoint. Finally, run_experiment unifies the entire execution workflow by applying hyperparameter overrides, computing class-balanced loss weights when required, evaluating models on the validation set, and visualizing loss and metric curves via plot_run.

  1. build_model: Dynamically builds the neural network with your chosen hidden layers, activation functions, dropout, and batch normalization.

  2. build_optimizer: Sets up the optimizer (like AdamW or SGD) using your learning rate, weight decay, and momentum settings.

  3. make_loaders: Converts the data splits into PyTorch DataLoaders with deterministic seeds for repeatable batches.

  4. fit: Manages the training loop, tracks losses and macro-F1 scores, applies early stopping, and keeps the best model weights.

  5. run_experiment: Orchestrates the whole process by handling overrides, calculating class weights, training the model, and printing results.

  6. plot_run: Draws the training and validation loss curves alongside the validation macro-F1 progress across epochs.

In [9]:
# Network builder: for each hidden layer Linear -> [BatchNorm] -> activation -> [Dropout].
# The last Linear layer gives one score per class.
def build_model(n_in, n_out, hidden_sizes=(64,), activation="relu", dropout=0.0, batchnorm=False):
    acts = {"relu": nn.ReLU, "linear": nn.Identity}
    layers, prev = [], n_in
    for h in hidden_sizes:
        layers.append(nn.Linear(prev, h))
        if batchnorm: layers.append(nn.BatchNorm1d(h))
        layers.append(acts[activation]())
        if dropout > 0: layers.append(nn.Dropout(dropout))
        prev = h
    layers.append(nn.Linear(prev, n_out))
    return nn.Sequential(*layers)

# Optimizer chosen by name. Both optimizers receive the weight decay.
def build_optimizer(params, name, lr, weight_decay, momentum):
    if name == "adamw": return optim.AdamW(params, lr=lr, weight_decay=weight_decay)
    if name == "sgd":   return optim.SGD(params, lr=lr, momentum=momentum, weight_decay=weight_decay)
    raise ValueError(name)

def make_loaders(data, scale, batch_size, seed):
    # Use the scaled features or the raw ones.
    X = data["X"] if scale else data["Xraw"]
    mk = lambda s: TensorDataset(torch.tensor(X[s], dtype=torch.float32),
                                 torch.tensor(data["y"][s], dtype=torch.long))
    # Fixed seed: the batches are the same at every run.
    # Validation is never shuffled and uses a bigger batch.
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    return (DataLoader(mk("train"), batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True, generator=g),
            DataLoader(mk("val"), batch_size=1024, shuffle=False))

# Loss and predictions on a whole split, without updating the weights.
def evaluate(model, loader, criterion):
    model.eval(); loss_sum, preds, labs = 0.0, [], []
    with torch.no_grad():
        for x, y in loader:
            x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
            out = model(x)
            loss_sum += criterion(out, y).item() * x.size(0)
            preds.append(out.argmax(1).cpu().numpy()); labs.append(y.cpu().numpy())
    return loss_sum / len(loader.dataset), np.concatenate(labs), np.concatenate(preds)

# Training loop with early stopping on the validation loss.
def fit(model, train_loader, val_loader, criterion, optimizer, epochs, patience, min_delta, restore_best=True):
    h = dict(train_loss=[], val_loss=[], val_f1=[])
    best, best_state, best_epoch, wait, t0 = float("inf"), None, 0, 0, time.time()
    for ep in range(epochs):
        model.train(); run = 0.0
        for x, y in train_loader:
            x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss = criterion(model(x), y)
            loss.backward(); optimizer.step()
            run += loss.item() * x.size(0)
        h["train_loss"].append(run / len(train_loader.dataset))
        vl, vt, vp = evaluate(model, val_loader, criterion)
        h["val_loss"].append(vl)
        h["val_f1"].append(f1_score(vt, vp, average="macro", zero_division=0))
        # Improvement: keep a copy of the weights on the CPU (cheaper than the GPU).
        if vl < best - min_delta:
            best, best_epoch, wait = vl, ep, 0
            best_state = {k: v.detach().cpu().clone() for k, v in model.state_dict().items()}
        else:
            wait += 1
            if wait >= patience: break
    # Put back the weights of the best epoch.
    if restore_best and best_state is not None: model.load_state_dict(best_state)
    h.update(best_epoch=best_epoch, n_epochs=len(h["train_loss"]), time_s=time.time() - t0)
    return h

# Default configuration. run_experiment can override any of these values.
DEFAULTS = dict(scale=True, hidden_sizes=(64,), activation="relu", dropout=0.0, batchnorm=False,
                optimizer="adamw", lr=5e-4, weight_decay=0.01, momentum=0.0,
                batch_size=64, epochs=100, patience=10, min_delta=1e-5,
                class_weight=None, seed=SEED, restore_best=True)

def run_experiment(task, change, data=None, plot=True, **overrides):
    """Run one experiment: build, train, evaluate and plot."""
    # Reject unknown parameter names, so a typo does not pass silently.
    unknown = set(overrides) - set(DEFAULTS)
    assert not unknown, f"unknown parameters: {unknown}"
    # Defaults + overrides = configuration of this run.
    cfg = {**DEFAULTS, **overrides}
    data = data or D
    names, n_cls = data["class_names"], len(data["class_names"])

    set_seed(cfg["seed"])
    tr, va = make_loaders(data, cfg["scale"], cfg["batch_size"], cfg["seed"])
    n_in = next(iter(tr))[0].shape[1]
    model = build_model(n_in, n_cls, cfg["hidden_sizes"], cfg["activation"],
                        cfg["dropout"], cfg["batchnorm"]).to(device)
    # Balanced loss: the rare classes get a bigger weight.
    w = None
    if cfg["class_weight"] == "balanced":
        c = np.bincount(data["y"]["train"], minlength=n_cls)
        w = torch.tensor(len(data["y"]["train"]) / (n_cls * c), dtype=torch.float32).to(device)
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(weight=w)
    opt = build_optimizer(model.parameters(), cfg["optimizer"], cfg["lr"],
                          cfg["weight_decay"], cfg["momentum"])

    # Train the model.
    h = fit(model, tr, va, criterion, opt, cfg["epochs"], cfg["patience"], cfg["min_delta"], cfg["restore_best"])

    vl, vt, vp = evaluate(model, va, nn.CrossEntropyLoss())

    # Per-class report and confusion matrix on the validation split.
    print(f"=== {task} | {change} ===")

    report_dict = classification_report(vt, vp, target_names=names, digits=3, zero_division=0, output_dict=True)
    accuracy_val = report_dict.pop("accuracy")

    print(f"Overall Accuracy: {accuracy_val:.3f}\n")
    report_df = pd.DataFrame(report_dict).T.round(3)
    display(report_df)

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4.5))
    cm = confusion_matrix(vt, vp)
    disp = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix=cm, display_labels=names)
    disp.plot(ax=ax, cmap="Blues", values_format="d")
    plt.title(f"Confusion Matrix - {task}")
    plt.grid(False)
    plt.show()

    # Best epoch is stored 0-based; the printout and the plots use it as an index.
    print(f"Best epoch: {h['best_epoch'] + 1} | epochs run: {h['n_epochs']} | time: {h['time_s']:.1f} s")

    # Loss and macro-F1 curves.
    if plot:
        plot_run(h, f"{task}\n{change}")

    return dict(model=model, hist=h, cfg=cfg, y_true=vt, y_pred=vp)

# Two plots: loss (train vs validation) and macro-F1 on validation.
def plot_run(h, title, logy=False):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.2))
    ax[0].plot(h["train_loss"], label="Train"); ax[0].plot(h["val_loss"], label="Val")
    ax[0].axvline(h["best_epoch"], ls="--", color="gray", label="Best epoch")
    ax[0].set(xlabel="Epoch", ylabel="Loss", title=title); ax[0].legend(); ax[0].grid(alpha=.3)
    if logy: ax[0].set_yscale("log")
    ax[1].plot(h["val_f1"], color="green"); ax[1].axvline(h["best_epoch"], ls="--", color="gray")
    ax[1].set(xlabel="Epoch", ylabel="Macro-F1 (val)", title="Macro-F1 validation"); ax[1].grid(alpha=.3)
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

4. Task 2¶

In this task, we test our framework with very simple examples. We mainly use the run_experiment function for this and future tasks.

4.1. Task 2A¶

In this task, we try our first simple baseline. This baseline is described by the default configuration of the run_experiment function

Q: How do you pick the "best" model across epochs? Do the curves converge?

Best model = lowest validation loss, checked every epoch, patience 10, best weights restored. Yes: both curves fall and flatten; the best epoch is 96 of 100, with validation loss 0.027, accuracy 0.992 and macro-F1 0.983.

Q: Do your hardest-class predictions hold up? Explain the per-class results.

Prediction: Brute Force (4.9% of the flows) would be the hardest. Only partly: its F1 is the lowest (0.953) but its recall is 0.995 and its precision 0.914, so the model misses almost no Brute Force flow; it pays for that with false positives (precision 0.914) on flows that look like Brute Force. Benign has the lowest recall (0.990) for the same reason: 10.5% of the Benign flows also use port 80. The network is using the port as a shortcut, which Task 3 tests directly.

Q: Rank S1–S3 by how badly they hurt, and which fundamental would you fix first on a new problem?

Validation macro-F1: S3 (lr 5e-6) 0.893 < S2 (lr 0.5) 0.910 < S1 (no scaling) 0.921, against 0.983 for the baseline. Brute Force F1 falls in the same order (0.814, 0.770, 0.846), so the ranking is not driven by one class. Scaling comes first: it is a property of the data that no learning rate can fix, and with features spanning 1 to $10^8$ the same step is enormous for one feature and negligible for another.

Q (reading symptoms): what in the shape of the curve would point you to the cause?

  • No scaling (S1): a slow, noisy descent that reaches a high plateau (about 2,000 instead of 0.03) and a validation macro-F1 that swings between 0.55 and 0.92; the loss jumps at every step because the large-range features dominate the gradient.
  • Learning rate too high (S2): the loss oscillates between 0 and 22 and never settles; early stopping fires after 15 epochs and the best one is epoch 5. The mechanism is that each step overshoots the minimum and the network keeps being thrown out of it.
  • Learning rate too low (S3): a smooth, slowly decaying curve that is still descending when the budget ends (best epoch 100 of 100). The mechanism is that the direction is right but the progress per step is 100x too small to reach the minimum in the budget.

To evaluate the performance of the new model on the test set, we define a new function eval_split, that specifically evaluates the model on the validation or test split without training.

In [15]:
def eval_split(model, data, split="test", scale=True, verbose=True):
    # Pick the requested split, scaled or raw.
    X = (data["X"] if scale else data["Xraw"])[split]
    y = data["y"][split]
    ds = TensorDataset(torch.tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32), torch.tensor(y, dtype=torch.long))
    # Loss, true labels and predictions for the whole split.
    loss, yt, yp = evaluate(model, DataLoader(ds, batch_size=1024, shuffle=False),
                            nn.CrossEntropyLoss())
    names = data["class_names"]
    # Print the per-class table and the confusion matrix.
    if verbose:
        print(f"--- {split.upper()} (loss {loss:.4f}) ---")
        report_dict = classification_report(yt, yp, target_names=names, digits=3, zero_division=0, output_dict=True)
        report_df = pd.DataFrame(report_dict).T
        report_df.index.name = None
        display(report_df.round(3))

        cm = confusion_matrix(yt, yp)
        cmd = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix=cm, display_labels=names)
        cmd.plot(cmap="Blues", xticks_rotation="vertical")
        plt.show()

    # Numbers used to compare the models.
    return dict(
        loss=loss,
        macro_f1=f1_score(yt, yp, average="macro"),
        recall=recall_score(yt, yp, average=None, labels=range(len(names)), zero_division=0)
    )

We then ran the evaluation on the validation set and the test set, filling the performance gap. A minimal performance gap confirms that the model generalizes well to unseen network traffic and has not overfitted to the validation set.

In [16]:

}, index=["loss", "macro_F1"] + [f"recall_{n}" for n in D["class_names"]]).round(4)

cmp["gap"] = (cmp["test"] - cmp["val"]).round(4)
cmp.index.name = None

print ("Comparison table")
display(cmp)

Q: Compare validation vs test. Does the model generalize?

Yes: validation 0.992 accuracy / 0.983 macro-F1, test 0.992 / 0.983, with gaps of +0.0009 in loss and -0.0003 in macro-F1; Brute Force recall is 0.995 on validation and 1.000 on test. The 300-epoch baseline is not overfitted to validation. The extra 200 epochs, however, bought nothing: the 100-epoch run already reached the same 0.983.

Q: Does the activation change the per-class results? Would it be fair to compare ReLU and linear on the test set?

Yes: switching from ReLU to linear drops macro-F1 from 0.983 to 0.922, Brute Force F1 from 0.953 to 0.797 (recall 0.995 -> 0.836) and DoS Hulk from 0.989 to 0.922, so the non-linearity mainly helps the two port-80 attack classes. Choosing the winner on the test set would not be fair: the test set must stay untouched until the model is fixed, otherwise the reported score has already been used to select the model.

5. Task 3¶

The objective of this section is to determine whether certain attack types (e.g., port scan) are strongly correlated with specific destination port numbers. Identifying this correlation reveals whether the model might heavily rely on port numbers rather than behavioral network traffic features and checks if the port distributions in the test set mirror those seen during training.

Q: Is "Brute Force always on port 80" a property of brute-force attacks in general, or an artefact of this dataset? If the model sees this, what is it likely to learn?

An artefact: 100% of the Brute Force training flows and 100% of DoS Hulk use port 80, while Benign uses it only 10.5% of the time; brute-force attacks also exist on SSH, FTP or RDP. The network will learn a shortcut ("port 80 means attack"), not the behaviour of the attack.

This next test modifies all Brute Force test samples targeting port 80 by reassigning them to port 8080, creating a modified version of our dataset

In [19]:
# Counterfactual test: move the Brute Force flows from port 80 to port 8080.
Xte_cf = D["Xraw"]["test"].copy()
mask = (D["y"]["test"] == bf) & (Xte_cf[:, port_idx] == 80)

print("BF samples shifted to 8080:", int(mask.sum()), "out of", int((D["y"]["test"] == bf).sum()))

Xte_cf[mask, port_idx] = 8080
# Apply the same transform used during training.
Xte_cf_scaled = D["scaler"].transform(Xte_cf)

BF samples shifted to 8080: 214 out of 214

We then define the eval_arrays function as a utility that evaluates a trained PyTorch model directly on arrays without manual tensor conversion. It displays clean per-class metric tables and plots the confusion matrix. With this function, we evaluate the model on the modified dataset, performing a counterfactual test

In [20]:
# Same evaluation as eval_split, but on plain arrays.
def eval_arrays(model, X, y, names):
    ds = TensorDataset(torch.tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32), torch.tensor(y, dtype=torch.long))
    loss, yt, yp = evaluate(model, DataLoader(ds, batch_size=1024, shuffle=False), nn.CrossEntropyLoss())

    report_dict = classification_report(yt, yp, target_names=names, digits=3, zero_division=0, output_dict=True)
    acc = report_dict.pop("accuracy")
    macro_avg = report_dict.pop("macro avg")
    weighted_avg = report_dict.pop("weighted avg")

    # One line with the main numbers.
    print(f"Evaluation Loss: {loss:.4f} | Accuracy: {acc:.3f} | Macro F1: {macro_avg['f1-score']:.3f}\n")

    report_df = pd.DataFrame(report_dict).T.round(3)
    display(report_df)

    # Confusion matrix.
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4.5))
    cm = confusion_matrix(yt, yp)
    disp = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix=cm, display_labels=names)
    disp.plot(ax=ax, cmap="Blues", values_format="d")
    plt.title("Confusion Matrix - Counterfactual Test")
    plt.grid(False)
    plt.show()

    return yt, yp

yt, yp = eval_arrays(BASE["model"], Xte_cf_scaled, D["y"]["test"], names)

Q: Did your prediction hold? What does this reveal about what the model was really using to detect Brute Force?

Prediction: Brute Force recall would collapse. It held: recall 1.000 -> 0.000 (F1 0.000), accuracy 0.992 -> 0.943 and macro-F1 0.983 -> 0.736, only because 214 test flows moved from port 80 to 8080 with no retraining. The model was reading the destination port, not the traffic shape.

Q: Count the classes after cleaning now, and compare to before. Which class shrinks when the port is removed and duplicates are dropped, and by how much?

With the port: 29384 flows (Benign 19240, Brute Force 1427, DoS Hulk 3868, PortScan 4849). Without port, de-duplicated: 22468 flows (Benign 16888, Brute Force 1427, DoS Hulk 3868, PortScan 285). PortScan loses 94.1% (4849 -> 285) and Benign 12.2%, while the other two classes do not move.

Q: Why does that class collapse while the others barely move? What does that tell you about what the model "knew" about that class?

A PortScan flow is one connection attempt per port: without the port, thousands of them become the same row and de-duplication keeps only 285. The other classes differ in volumes and timings, so their rows stay unique. Before, PortScan looked large and easy because it counted near-copies of the same behaviour.

We define D2 as the sanitized dataset without the destination port feature and with deduplication applied. The dataset D2 will be used for the rest of the lab

In [22]:
D2 = D_nodup

classes = D2["class_names"]
# Number of samples per class in each split.
split_dist = pd.DataFrame({
    "Train": np.bincount(D2["y"]["train"], minlength=len(classes)),
    "Val":   np.bincount(D2["y"]["val"], minlength=len(classes)),
    "Test":  np.bincount(D2["y"]["test"], minlength=len(classes))
}, index=classes)

split_dist["Total"] = split_dist.sum(axis=1)
split_dist.loc["TOTAL"] = split_dist.sum(axis=0)
split_dist.index.name = None

print("Class Distribution Across Splits (D2):")
display(split_dist)

Q: After dropping the port, which class is now the rarest? How balanced is the data now?

PortScan, with 285 flows (1.3%), against Brute Force 1427 (6.4%), DoS Hulk 3868 (17.2%) and Benign 16888 (75.2%). The imbalance is much worse than before removing the port, when the rarest class was 4.9%.

Q: Knowing that de-duplication decimates one class once the port is gone, do you still de-duplicate?

Yes. Duplicate rows are the same flow copied, not independent evidence: keeping them inflates the metrics and puts identical rows in train and test. We keep the 285 distinct PortScan flows and compensate with class weights in Task 4.

Q: Can you still detect the rarest class at all?

Yes. On validation, without class weights: PortScan recall 0.907, precision 0.975, F1 0.940 (43 flows in validation, 199 in training), accuracy 0.982 and macro-F1 0.959. The class is rare but not lost, because its behaviour is still different from the other classes.

Caveat for all the numbers of Tasks 4-6: validation and test contain only 43 PortScan flows each, so one flow moves its recall by 2.3 points. Differences below ~0.05 macro-F1 are one or two flows and are not reliable with a single seed.

Then, we change our loss function to a class-weighted cross-entropy loss (balanced weights) and train again.

In [24]:
r8 = run_experiment("4B", "Weighted Loss (balanced)", data=D2, class_weight="balanced", **BASE_OVERRIDES)

=== 4B | Weighted Loss (balanced) ===
Overall Accuracy: 0.955
precision recall f1-score support
Benign 0.997 0.946 0.970 2533.0
Brute Force 0.818 0.986 0.894 214.0
DoS Hulk 0.922 0.983 0.952 580.0
PortScan 0.462 0.977 0.627 43.0
macro avg 0.800 0.973 0.861 3370.0
weighted avg 0.966 0.955 0.958 3370.0 
Best epoch: 63 | epochs run: 73 | time: 15.4 s

Q: From which partition do you compute the class weights, and why would using another partition be wrong?

From the training split of D2 only (np.bincount on data["y"]["train"], 15727 flows). Weights computed on validation or test would encode the evaluation distribution into the loss and bias the numbers used to judge the model.

Q: Did accuracy and macro-F1 move in the same direction? Which metric should an intrusion detector optimize?

Both fell: accuracy 0.982 -> 0.960 and macro-F1 0.959 -> 0.884, while rare-class recall rose (PortScan 0.907 -> 0.977, Brute Force 0.939 -> 0.986) and PortScan precision fell from 0.975 to 0.553. The weights therefore buy recall, not macro-F1: they trade many false alarms for few missed attacks. Accuracy is dominated by Benign (75%), so it is the wrong headline; an intrusion detector should optimize rare-class recall (or macro-F1) and then choose the operating point on a precision/recall curve, because a missed attack costs more than a false alarm.

7. Task 5¶

In this task, we evaluate if more complex models can beat our baseline.

We establish a new baseline. It maintains the exact model architecture and hyperparameters as the original setup, modified only by adjusting the loss function to handle class imbalance (it is the same model used in the last section of Task 4)

Q: Does depth help on this problem? If a single-hidden-layer baseline stays competitive, what does that suggest about the complexity of this task?

Only the width helps. At width 64, one layer gives 0.884, two layers 0.901 and three layers 0.897: the second layer buys +0.017 and the third -0.004, so depth buys nothing. The gain comes from widening: (128,64,32) reaches 0.925, +0.028 over (64,32). All of them are above the weighted single-layer baseline (0.884) but below the unweighted one (0.959), and the gap between those two baselines is larger than anything depth adds. This suggests a low-dimensional, largely separable task in which a single hidden layer already has enough capacity.

Q: Report validation results and training time, and explain both.

Batch val macro-F1 best epoch epochs run weight updates time
16 0.899 50 60 ~59k 133.5 s
128 0.868 99 109 ~13k 45.2 s
1024 0.866 293 300 ~5k 48.7 s

The small batch is the slowest (2.2 s per epoch against 0.4 and 0.2) because each epoch contains 983 weight updates instead of 123 or 16, and it generalizes best. The largest batch is the cheapest per epoch but needs 300 epochs to reach a worse value: over the whole run it sees only ~5k updates, about 12x fewer than batch 16, so part of its gap is optimization budget, not the batch size itself. The three scores are within the noise of 43 PortScan flows, so only the ordering of the times is solid.

Q: What did you find - does the optimizer or the learning rate dominate on this data?

Neither in a clean way: the runs cannot fully separate them. Inside SGD the learning rate is the main lever: 10x it (0.01 -> 0.1) and macro-F1 goes 0.787 -> 0.817 (+0.030) in 27 epochs instead of 130; momentum 0.9 at lr 0.01 changes nothing measurable (0.781, -0.006). But with the same weight decay AdamW reaches 0.897, +0.080 over the best SGD: here the optimizer/weight-decay combination moves the result more than any learning-rate step. Two caveats: r18 changes the optimizer and the lr together, so it cannot attribute the gain; and weight decay is not the same operation in the two optimizers (decoupled in AdamW, L2 added to the gradient in SGD), which is why the SGD runs underfit with wd 0.01. The honest conclusion is that the learning rate is what you tune inside a fixed optimizer, but the optimizer choice sets the level you can reach.

7.4. Task 5D¶

We take the best model of the ones we trained in this task and put it against our initial baseline. The model of choice is r11

In [36]:
# Evaluate several models on the same split.
def compare_models(models, data=D2, split="test"):
    results = {}

    for name, exp in models.items():
        print("=" * 12, name, "=" * 12)
        results[name] = eval_split(exp["model"], data, split)

    results_df = pd.DataFrame({
        name: [res["loss"], res["macro_f1"], *res["recall"]]
        for name, res in results.items()
    }, index=["loss", "macro_F1"] + [f"recall_{n}" for n in data["class_names"]])
    results_df.index.name = None

    print("Comparison table")
    display(results_df.round(4))

Q: Did the added complexity beat the simple baseline? Was it worth the runs it cost?

Against the weighted baseline, yes: test macro-F1 0.928 vs 0.871 and accuracy 0.966 vs 0.952, with the gain in PortScan (precision 0.532 -> 0.808) and DoS Hulk. Against the simple port-free baseline of Task 4 (r7, the unweighted model, test macro-F1 0.957 / accuracy 0.980) no: the deeper model is 0.029 below it. The weighted loss had already cost 0.086, and the extra depth only recovered 0.057 of that. Three runs of Task 5A for a model that does not beat the simpler one: the complexity was not worth it.

This task deals with overfitting problems and how to minimize them.

Q: Is it overfitting? Show exactly where you see it in the curves.

Mildly, and the curves show exactly where. Up to epoch ~45 the train and validation losses fall together; the minimum of the validation loss is at epoch 44. After that the training loss keeps falling (to ~0.03) while the validation loss rises steadily (to ~0.19 at epoch 200): the extra 156 epochs only make the model fit the training flows. The table, computed with the unweighted loss, shows a smaller gap with the same shape (train 0.058, validation 0.072); accuracy is almost identical (train 0.978, validation 0.979) but PortScan recall is 1.000 on train against 0.954 on validation, so the memorisation is concentrated in the rarest class. The two losses differ because fit evaluates with the weighted criterion used for training, while eval_split uses an unweighted one.

Now that we confirmed overfitting, we can start mitigating it. The first countermeasure we implement is early stopping. We define a new configuration T6A

In [39]:

Q: Which change helped the most for the least effort?

Early stopping: it cuts the run from 200 to 25 epochs (4.9 s instead of 129 s) and keeps validation macro-F1 at 0.919, 0.032 below the unregularized run. Among the regularizers, dropout 0.24 gives the best validation score (0.923, +0.004 over early stopping) for ~10 s; weight decay adds nothing (0.921) and batch normalization costs a run and lowers the score (0.907). On test the dropout net reaches 0.929 macro-F1, the best of the Task 6 models, while the smaller 1x64 net reaches 0.924. All the differences between the regularized variants are within the noise of 43 PortScan flows, so the ranking is: early stopping first, then dropout if one more run is available, and no batch normalization.

In conclusion, we compare the Task 4 baseline r8 with the best regularized 5-layer network of Task 6 (r22, chosen on validation) and with the smaller one-layer network r24.

Q: In the end, did the big network - even with regularization - do better on the test set than the simple port-free baseline?

No, if the baseline is the unweighted port-free model r7 (test macro-F1 0.957 / accuracy 0.980): the regularized 5-layer net r22 reaches 0.929 / 0.964 and the smaller r24 0.924 / 0.966. Yes, if the baseline is the weighted r8 (0.871 / 0.952), which is the model Task 4 ends with: r22 is +0.058. The per-class detail explains the gap: the 5-layer net finds PortScan more often (recall 1.000 vs 0.884) but with more false alarms (precision 0.827 vs 0.974), and it is worse on Brute Force (F1 0.882 vs 0.949). Regularization and early stopping recovered about two thirds of the 0.086 that the weighted loss had cost (0.871 -> 0.929), but the plain 1x64 unweighted model stays ahead of every 5-layer network. With 43 PortScan flows in test, differences of a few points are one or two flows.

Q: Looking across the whole logbook, which decisions gave the most performance per unit of effort?

The data decisions, not the models. Stratifying the split and applying log1p + StandardScaler moved validation macro-F1 from 0.921 (no scaling) to 0.983 with a few lines of code, and no architecture change came close to that. Removing the port cost 0.024 macro-F1, but the shortcut it removed was worth all of Brute Force recall (1.000 -> 0.000 when only the port was changed in Task 3). Class weights bought rare-class recall (PortScan 0.907 -> 0.977) at the price of macro-F1 (0.959 -> 0.884). Depth, width, batch size, optimizer and regularizers each moved macro-F1 by at most ~0.04, and the best of them did not beat the simple baseline: those were the least efficient runs.
